claim: Male Wistar rats emit 44-kHz ultrasonic vocalizations during prolonged Pavlovian fear conditioning.
source: Here, we describe aversive vocalizations emitted at a higher pitch by male Wistar and spontaneously hypertensive rats (SHR) in an intensified aversive state – prolonged fear conditioning. These calls, which we named '44-kHz' vocalizations, are long (>150 ms), generally at a constant frequency (usually within 35–50-kHz range) and have an overall spectrographic image similar to 22-kHz calls.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the observation of 44-kHz vocalizations in male Wistar rats during prolonged fear conditioning experiments.

claim: 44-kHz vocalizations can be sorted into five subtypes: flat, step up, step down, insert, and complex.
source: Based on the composition of individual call elements and their relation to each other, we manually sorted the calls into five categories (Figure 2B–F). If the start (prefix) or end (suffix) portion of a call was less than 1/5th the length of the following or previous element, this portion of the call was not considered in its categorization into the five subtypes. The names and descriptions of the five subtypes are: flat – single element with near constant frequency and little to no interruptions to the sound continuity on the spectrogram; step up – two elements with an instantaneous frequency jump, where the first element is of lower frequency; step down – two elements with an instantaneous frequency jump, where the first element is of higher frequency; insert – three elements with an instantaneous frequency change, where the middle element is of different frequency; and complex – more than three elements with instantaneous frequency changes.
evidence: This is a classification scheme developed through manual analysis of vocalization structure.

source: Specifically, in 14 rats (13 Wistar and 1 SHR) with a clear transition from 22-kHz to 44-kHz calls during the fear conditioning training session (n = 14, selected from Table 1/Exp. 1–3/#2,4,6–8,10–13), the proportion between the frequencies of the long 22-kHz vocalizations and the long 44-kHz calls was 1.48 ± 0.02.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from frequency analysis of vocalization transitions.

claim: For 70 step up calls, the frequency ratio was 1.53 ± 0.03.
source: Similar results were obtained for 70 step up (1.53 ± 0.03) and 65 step down (1.59 ± 0.02) 44-kHz calls
evidence: This is a quantitative result from frequency analysis of specific call subtypes.

claim: For 65 step down calls, the frequency ratio was 1.59 ± 0.02.
source: Similar results were obtained for 70 step up (1.53 ± 0.03) and 65 step down (1.59 ± 0.02) 44-kHz calls
evidence: This is a quantitative result from frequency analysis of specific call subtypes.

claim: The 3:2 frequency ratio has been observed in invertebrates and vertebrates including human speech and music.
source: This ratio and its relevance have been observed in invertebrates and vertebrates including human speech and music (Hoeschele, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the broader significance of the frequency ratio, supported by citation.

claim: In music theory, 3:2 frequency ratio is referred to as a perfect fifth.
source: In music theory, 3:2 frequency ratio is referred to as a perfect fifth and is often featured, for example, the first two notes of the Star Wars 1977 movie (ascending, i.e., step up; comp. Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1) and Game of Thrones 2011 television series (descending, i.e., step down; comp. Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2) theme songs.
evidence: This is a statement about music theory and examples from popular culture.

claim: All physical objects capable of producing tonal sounds generate harmonic vibrations, the most prominent being the octave, perfect fifth, and major third.
source: All of these may point to a common basis for this sound interval and its prevalence that could be explained by the observation that all physical objects capable of producing tonal sounds generate harmonic vibrations, the most prominent being the octave, perfect fifth, and major third (Christensen, 1993, discussed in Bowling and Purves, 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the physical basis of harmonic intervals, supported by citations.

claim: DBSCAN algorithm divided all vocalizations into 44-kHz vocalizations vs. all other vocalizations as two separate clusters.
source: Next, we showed that 44-kHz calls indeed constitute a separable type of ultrasonic vocalizations as it was sorted into isolated clusters by two different methods. First, using the DBSCAN algorithm method based on calls' peak frequency and duration, we were able to divide all vocalizations recorded during all training sessions into 44-kHz vocalizations vs. all other vocalizations as two separate clusters (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from clustering analysis demonstrating separability of 44-kHz calls.

claim: k-means clustering with UMAP sorted 44-kHz vocalizations of different subtypes into topologically-separate groups.
source: Secondly, a clustering algorithm that includes call contours, that is, k-means with UMAP done via DeepSqueak (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), sorted 44-kHz vocalizations of different subtypes including unusual ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–F), into topologically-separate groups.
evidence: This is a result from clustering analysis demonstrating separability of 44-kHz call subtypes.

claim: Flat 44-kHz calls were consistently in a separate cluster from 22-kHz calls.
source: Notably, flat 44-kHz calls were consistently in a separate cluster from 22-kHz calls (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from clustering analysis showing consistent separation of flat 44-kHz calls.

claim: The most probable call following long 22-kHz vocalization was another long 22-kHz vocalization (94.4% probability).
source: The most probable call following long 22-kHz vocalization was another long 22-kHz vocalization (94.4% probability).
evidence: This is a result from transition probability analysis of call sequences.

claim: The most probable call following 44-kHz vocalization was another 44-kHz call (83.1%).
source: Similarly, the most probable call following 44-kHz vocalization was another 44-kHz call (83.1%).
evidence: This is a result from transition probability analysis of call sequences.

claim: When analysis was limited to vocalizations emitted only in bouts, transition probabilities reached 96.3% for 22-kHz calls and 86.5% for 44-kHz calls.
source: These values augmented when the analysis was limited to vocalizations emitted only in bouts, that is, with <320 ms time gaps between calls (Wöhr et al., 2005), and reached 96.3 and 86.5%, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from transition probability analysis restricted to bout vocalizations.

claim: The heart rate of rats exposed to 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations decreased.
source: For example, the heart rate of rats exposed to 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations decreased, and increased to 50-kHz calls (Figure 4A, comp. Olszyński et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring physiological responses.

claim: The heart rate of rats exposed to 50-kHz vocalizations increased.
source: For example, the heart rate of rats exposed to 22-kHz and 44-kHz vocalizations decreased, and increased to 50-kHz calls (Figure 4A, comp. Olszyński et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring physiological responses.

claim: The number of vocalizations emitted by rats was highest during and after the playback of 50-kHz calls.
source: Whereas the number of vocalizations emitted by rats was the highest during and after the playback of 50-kHz, intermediate to 44-kHz and lowest to 22-kHz playbacks (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring vocal responses.

claim: The number of vocalizations emitted by rats was intermediate in response to 44-kHz playback.
source: Whereas the number of vocalizations emitted by rats was the highest during and after the playback of 50-kHz, intermediate to 44-kHz and lowest to 22-kHz playbacks (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring vocal responses.

claim: The number of vocalizations emitted by rats was lowest in response to 22-kHz playback.
source: Whereas the number of vocalizations emitted by rats was the highest during and after the playback of 50-kHz, intermediate to 44-kHz and lowest to 22-kHz playbacks (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring vocal responses.

claim: The duration of 50-kHz vocalizations emitted in response to 44-kHz playback was longer than following 22-kHz playback.
source: Additionally, the duration of 50-kHz vocalizations emitted in response to 44-kHz playback was also intermediate, that is, longer than following 22-kHz playback (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring characteristics of emitted vocalizations.

claim: The duration of 50-kHz vocalizations emitted in response to 44-kHz playback was shorter than following 50-kHz playback.
source: and shorter than following 50-kHz playback (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring characteristics of emitted vocalizations.

claim: Similar tendencies were observed in the distance traveled and time spent in the half of the cage adjacent to the speaker during playback experiments.
source: Finally, similar tendencies were observed in the distance traveled and time spent in the half of the cage adjacent to the speaker (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is a result from playback experiments measuring locomotor and spatial responses.

claim: Frequency usually increases with an increase in arousal in animal vocalizations.
source: The frequency shifts toward both higher and lower levels, that is, alterations were observed during both positive (appetitive) and negative (agonistic/aversive) situations; however, as a general rule, frequency usually increases with an increase in arousal (Briefer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about general principles of animal vocal communication, supported by citation.

claim: Prolonged fear conditioning increased the arousal of the rats with no change in the valence of the aversive stimuli.
source: We would like to propose a hypothesis that our prolonged fear conditioning increased the arousal of the rats with no change in the valence of the aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis to explain the emergence of 44-kHz vocalizations.

claim: 44-kHz vocalizations communicate an increased negative emotional state.
source: However, several arguments support the idea that 44-kHz vocalizations communicate an increased negative emotional state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ultrasonic vocalizations serve as a means of communicating rats' emotional state.
source: First, in general, ultrasonic vocalizations serve as a means of communicating rats' emotional state (Brudzynski, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the function of rat vocalizations, supported by citation.

claim: 44-kHz calls were notably more frequent during prolonged aversive stimulation (5th–10th trials of fear conditioning training).
source: Third, 44-kHz calls were notably more frequent during prolonged aversive stimulation, that is, the 5th–10th trials of fear conditioning training.
evidence: This is a summary of the temporal pattern of 44-kHz call emission.

claim: 44-kHz calls appeared as partial replacements of 22-kHz calls in the presence of the same painful stimulus.
source: Fifth, they appeared as partial replacements of, established as aversive, 22-kHz calls – in the presence of the same painful stimulus.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between 44-kHz and 22-kHz calls during fear conditioning.

claim: Numerous instances of vocalizations featured both 22-kHz-like and 44-kHz-like call elements.
source: Sixth, numerous instances of vocalizations featured both 22-kHz-like and 44-kHz-like call elements.
evidence: This is an observation about the structure of some vocalizations.

claim: The sound mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations was comparable to, or possibly even higher than, that of 22-kHz calls.
source: Also, several observations contradict the potential contribution of fatigue. The sound mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations was comparable to, or possibly even higher than, that of 22-kHz calls, despite the higher energy costs associated with producing higher-pitched calls (Sonninen and Hurme, 1998)
evidence: This is a result from amplitude analysis, with citation supporting the energy cost claim.

claim: Producing higher-pitched calls has higher energy costs.
source: The sound mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations was comparable to, or possibly even higher than, that of 22-kHz calls, despite the higher energy costs associated with producing higher-pitched calls (Sonninen and Hurme, 1998)
evidence: This is a statement about vocal production physiology, supported by citation.

claim: Rats emitting 44-kHz calls invested additional energy to communicate their emotional state.
source: that is, the rats emitting 44-kHz calls invested additional energy to communicate their emotional state
evidence: This is an inference based on the amplitude and frequency characteristics of 44-kHz calls.

claim: Both in vivo measurements and computer modeling demonstrated that producing calls of higher frequency requires increased activity of various muscles.
source: both in vivo measurements (Riede, 2013) and computer modeling (Håkansson et al., 2022) demonstrated that producing calls of higher frequency, such as 50-kHz vs. 22-kHz, requires increased activity of various muscles.
evidence: This is a statement about vocal production physiology, supported by citations.

claim: The mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations remained strong and stable for several trials.
source: Additionally, the mean power of 44-kHz vocalizations remained strong and stable for several trials – in contrast to 22-kHz vocalizations.
evidence: This is a result from amplitude analysis over time.

claim: When 44-kHz calls started to appear in significant numbers (after the 4th–5th trials), they were as long as 22-kHz vocalizations.
source: Finally, when 44-kHz calls started to appear in significant numbers, that is, after the 4th–5th trials of fear conditioning training, they were as long as 22-kHz vocalizations.
evidence: This is a result from duration analysis of vocalizations.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the mean power of 22-kHz vocalizations during the fear conditioning training session.
source: Concerning the latter, we observed a significant decrease in the mean power of 22-kHz vocalizations during the fear conditioning training session.
evidence: This is a result from amplitude analysis over time.

claim: Reduction in amplitude could potentially be attributed to fatigue or despair.
source: Such reduction could potentially be attributed to fatigue (as observed in humans, Kitch and Oates, 1994), despair (e.g., as a reaction to the lack of effects from repeated emissions of 22-kHz calls), or both.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the amplitude reduction, with citation for the fatigue claim.

claim: The reduction in the amplitude of 22-kHz calls during 10-trial fear conditioning training was also recently observed by Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023.
source: The reduction in the amplitude of 22-kHz calls during the 10-trial fear conditioning training was also recently observed by others (Gonzalez-Palomares et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a citation of a recent publication that reported similar findings.

claim: Training rats with several electric foot-shocks (5–10 shocks) produces a qualitatively different kind of fear memory compared to training with only 1–2 shocks.
source: Importantly, it has been demonstrated multiple times that training rats with several electric foot-shocks (i.e., 5–10 shocks) produces a qualitatively different kind of fear memory compared to training with only 1–2 shocks.
evidence: This is a statement about established findings in fear conditioning research.

claim: Training with more numerous shocks results in augmented freezing.
source: Training with more numerous shocks has been shown to result in augmented freezing (e.g., Fanselow and Bolles, 1979; Haubrich et al., 2020; Haubrich and Nader, 2023; Poulos et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a statement about established findings in fear conditioning research, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Augmented freezing reflects a more intense fear memory that is resistant to extinction.
source: which reflects a more intense fear memory that is resistant to extinction (Haubrich et al., 2020; Haubrich and Nader, 2023)
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of fear memories formed with multiple shocks, supported by citations.

claim: Intense fear memory is resistant to reconsolidation blockade.
source: resistant to reconsolidation blockade (Haubrich et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2009; Finnie and Nader, 2020)
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of fear memories formed with multiple shocks, supported by citations.

claim: Intense fear memory is associated with downregulation of NR2B NMDA-receptor subunits in the lateral and basal amygdala.
source: associated with downregulation of NR2B NMDA-receptor subunits as well as elevated amyloid-beta concentrations in the lateral and basal amygdala (Finnie and Nader, 2020; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the molecular mechanisms of fear memories formed with multiple shocks, supported by citations.

claim: Intense fear memory is associated with elevated amyloid-beta concentrations in the lateral and basal amygdala.
source: associated with downregulation of NR2B NMDA-receptor subunits as well as elevated amyloid-beta concentrations in the lateral and basal amygdala (Finnie and Nader, 2020; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the molecular mechanisms of fear memories formed with multiple shocks, supported by citations.

claim: Intense fear memory involves activation of the noradrenaline-locus coeruleus system.
source: Additionally, it involves activation of the noradrenaline-locus coeruleus system (Haubrich et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a statement about the neural systems involved in fear memories formed with multiple shocks, supported by citation.

claim: Intense fear memory involves collective changes in connectivity across multiple brain regions within the neural network.
source: and collective changes in connectivity across multiple brain regions within the neural network (Haubrich and Nader, 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the neural mechanisms of fear memories formed with multiple shocks, supported by citation.

claim: Higher freezing as a result of fear conditioning training correlates with increased concentrations of stress hormone, corticosterone, in the blood.
source: Notably, it has also been shown that higher freezing as a result of fear conditioning training correlates with increased concentrations of stress hormone, corticosterone, in the blood (Dos Santos Corrêa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between freezing and stress hormones, supported by citation.

claim: Rats subjected to 6- and 10-trial fear conditioning training demonstrated higher freezing than rats subjected to 1-trial conditioning.
source: The rats subjected to 6- and 10-trial fear conditioning training, whose results are reported herein (Table 1/Exp. 2/#7,8,11,12; n = 73), also demonstrated higher freezing than rats subjected to 1-trial conditioning (Table 1/Exp. 2/#6,10; n = 33), which is reported elsewhere (Olszyński et al., 2021, Fig. S1C–E; Olszyński et al., 2023, Fig. S1D–G).
evidence: This is a comparative result from the experiments, with citations to previous publications.

claim: Emission of 44-kHz calls is associated with increased stress and the training regime forming robust memories.
source: Therefore, we postulate that emission of 44-kHz calls is associated with increased stress and the training regime forming robust memories.
evidence: This is a postulated interpretation based on the evidence presented.

claim: Rat ultrasonic vocalizations can alter emotional states in tested rats via playback of affectively valenced calls.
source: Amounting research points to the utility of rat ultrasonic vocalizations to alter emotional states, evidenced by behavioral changes, in tested rats via playback of affectively valenced calls (Bonauto et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional effects of rat vocalizations, supported by citation.

claim: Rats responded similarly to hearing 44-kHz calls as they did to hearing aversive 22-kHz calls, especially regarding heart rate change.
source: In general, the rats responded similarly to hearing 44-kHz calls as they did to hearing aversive 22-kHz calls, especially regarding heart rate change, despite the 44-kHz calls occupying the frequency band of appetitive 50-kHz vocalizations.
evidence: This is a summary of the playback experiment results.

claim: The similarity in responses to 44-kHz and 22-kHz calls is contrary to observations suggesting that frequency band plays the main role in rat ultrasound perception.
source: This is contrary to some observations (Saito et al., 2019), which suggested that frequency band plays the main role in rat ultrasound perception.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current findings with previous research, supported by citation.

claim: Long, frequency-stable high-pitch vocalizations have been reported before.
source: On one hand, long (or not that long as in Bialy et al., 2019), frequency-stable high-pitch vocalizations have been reported before (e.g., Sales, 1979; Shimoju et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a statement about previous reports of similar vocalizations, supported by citations.

claim: Long, frequency-stable high-pitch vocalizations have been caused by intense cholinergic stimulation.
source: notably as caused by intense cholinergic stimulation (Brudzynski and Bihari, 1990) or higher shock-dose fear conditioning (Wöhr et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about previous reports of similar vocalizations, supported by citations.

claim: Long, frequency-stable high-pitch vocalizations have been caused by higher shock-dose fear conditioning.
source: notably as caused by intense cholinergic stimulation (Brudzynski and Bihari, 1990) or higher shock-dose fear conditioning (Wöhr et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a statement about previous reports of similar vocalizations, supported by citations.

claim: Long, frequency-stable high-pitch vocalizations have not been systematically defined, described, fully shown, or demonstrated to be a separate type of vocalization prior to this study.
source: However, they have not been systematically defined, described, fully shown, or demonstrated to be a separate type of vocalization.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study's contribution.

claim: 44-kHz calls were likely omitted in previous studies because analyses were restricted to canonical groups with a sharp dividing frequency border.
source: On the other hand, 44-kHz calls were likely omitted as the analyses were restricted to canonical groups, that is, flat 22-kHz and short 50-kHz calls, with a sharp dividing frequency border between the two (e.g., Kalamari et al., 2021; Potasiewicz et al., 2020; Turner et al., 2019) or even a frequency 'safety gap' between 22-kHz and 50-kHz vocalizations (e.g., Silkstone and Brudzynski, 2019; Garcia et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an explanation for why 44-kHz calls may have been overlooked, with citations to examples.

claim: Many older bat detectors had limited frequency-range detection (up to 40-kHz) when stress-evoked types of ultrasonic calls were being established.
source: Moreover, many older bat detectors had limited frequency-range detection (e.g., up to 40-kHz in Sales, 1991) when stress-evoked types of ultrasonic calls were being established.
evidence: This is an explanation for why 44-kHz calls may have been overlooked, with citation to an example.

claim: 44-kHz vocalizations are emitted much fewer than 22-kHz calls.
source: Finally, 44-kHz vocalizations are emitted much fewer than 22-kHz calls (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is a summary of the relative frequency of different call types.

claim: 44-kHz vocalizations are a separate and behaviorally relevant group of rat ultrasonic calls.
source: Here, we present introductory evidence that 44-kHz vocalizations are a separate and behaviorally relevant group of rat ultrasonic calls.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Rats employ previously unrecognized, long, high-pitched and flat aversive calls in their vocal repertoire.
source: However, our results bring to awareness that rats employ these previously unrecognized, long, high-pitched and flat aversive calls in their vocal repertoire.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: Researchers investigating rat ultrasonic vocalizations should be aware of the potential presence of 44-kHz calls.
source: Researchers investigating rat ultrasonic vocalizations should be aware of their potential presence and to not rely fully on automated detection of high- vs. low-pitch calls.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Researchers should not rely fully on automated detection of high- vs. low-pitch calls.
source: Researchers investigating rat ultrasonic vocalizations should be aware of their potential presence and to not rely fully on automated detection of high- vs. low-pitch calls.
